newsitem.title: UK: UK sales data give Clarke breathing space on rates.
newsitem.headline: UK sales data give Clarke breathing space on rates.

text.p: A sharp fall in British retail sales in December suggests that fears of a runaway boom are misplaced and may allow Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to get away with leaving interest rates on hold until the election.

"These figures definitely take the pressure off Clarke for a further monetary tightening," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS. "While sterling is depressing exports, the domestic economy is now showing signs of slowing of its own accord."
Retail sales fell 0.8 percent in December compared with a 0.8 percent rise in November.
The year-on-year rate of growth slowed to 2.9 percent from 4.0 percent in November.
Economists said while the Bank of England is still likely to battle for a rate rise, the sales data could rob it of some powerful ammunition.

"The Bank's line has been that while sterling may be depressing exports, it will do nothing to slow consumer activity. So any further signs that demand is slowing independently will leave the Bank with fewer arguments for a tightening," said Garrard.
Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International, said the Bank will probably stick to the same line, but use other data from the consumer sector to back its case for a tighening.

"The Governor will say that if you look at the underlying picture, not just retail sales but the broader consumer spending picture, taking in the housing market and auto sales, it is actually still quite strong."

But he thinks Clarke will now have another reason to overrule the Bank. "It is very dangerous to rule out anything, but the data obviously shift the argument further to the view that Clarke will wait until after the election."
Clarke left rates on hold after the January 15 meeting with Governor Eddie George, saying the strength of sterling was a key factor in his decision.

But in a speech Monday George turned up the heat on Clarke, saying there were real dangers in allowing concern about the pound's effect on exports to deflect attention from the need to tighten policy. The two men meet again on February 5.
The retail sales data mirrored evidence from recent surveys which pointed to slowing demand for clothing and footwear. That sector saw a 4.6 percent monthly drop in turnover in December.
Analysts said this showed that despite increased wealth, consumers were still very sensitive to price rises.
"Consumers have punished retailers for recent price hikes in this area. At least some of these price rises could be reversed in coming months," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Retailers pushed up the price of clothing and footwear as demand grew in the autumn. RPI data showed prices in the sector rose 1.1 percent in November, although prices fell slightly in December.
